{{Short description|Topology procedure in mathematics}}

{{Orphan|date=January 2025}}
A '''hyperbolization procedure''' is a procedure that turns a [[polyhedral complex]] <math>K</math> into a [[non-positively curved space]] <math>\mathcal H (K)</math>, retaining some of its topological features. Roughly speaking, the procedure consists in replacing every cell of <math>K</math> with a copy of a certain non-positively curved manifold with boundary, which is fixed a priori and is called the '''hyperbolizing cell''' of the procedure.

There are many different hyperbolization procedures available in the literature. While they all satisfy some common axioms, they differ by what kind of polyhedral complex is allowed as input and what kind of hyperbolizing cell is used. As a result, different procedures preserve different topological features and provide spaces with different geometric flavors. The first hyperbolization procedures were introduced by [[Mikhael Gromov (mathematician)|Mikhael Gromov]] in <ref name=":1">{{cite book |last=Gromov |first=Mikhail |author-link=Mikhail Gromov (mathematician) |title=Essays in Group Theory |publisher=Springer |year=1987 |isbn=0-387-96618-8 |editor-last=Gersten |editor-first=Steve M. |series=Mathematical Sciences Research Institute Publications |volume=8 |location=New York |pages=75–263 |chapter=Hyperbolic Groups |doi=10.1007/978-1-4613-9586-7_3 |mr=919829}}</ref> and later other versions were developed by several mathematicians including [[Ruth Charney]], [[Michael W. Davis]], and [[Pedro Ontaneda]].

It is important to note that the word "hyperbolization" here does not have the same meaning that it has in the [[Uniformization theorem|uniformization]] or [[Hyperbolization theorem|hyperbolization]] results typical of low-dimensional geometry. Indeed, the space <math>\mathcal H (K)</math> is not homeomorphic to <math>K</math>. For instance, <math>\mathcal H (K)</math> is always [[Aspherical space|aspherical]], regardless of whether <math>K</math> is aspherical. Moreover, despite the name of the procedure, <math>\mathcal H (K)</math> is not always guaranteed to be negatively curved, so some authors refer to these procedures as asphericalization procedures.

== Axioms ==
An assignment <math>K \to \mathcal H (K)</math> is '''hyperbolization procedure''' if it satisfies the following properties:

# (''Non-positive curvature''). <math>\mathcal H (K)</math> admits a [[CAT(k) space|locally CAT(0)]] metric.
# (''Functoriality''). If <math>L\hookrightarrow K</math> is the inclusion of a subcomplex, then there is an isometric embedding <math>\mathcal H  (L) \hookrightarrow \mathcal H (K)</math> with locally convex image.
# (''Local structure is preserved''). If <math>\sigma^n</math> is an <math>n</math>-cell of <math>K</math>, then <math>\mathcal H (\sigma^n)</math> is a connected <math>n</math>-manifold with boundary and the link of <math>\mathcal H (\sigma^n)</math> in <math>\mathcal H (K)</math> is isomorphic to the link of <math>\sigma^n</math> in <math>K</math>, possibly up to subdivisions. 
# (''Homology is enriched''). The map <math>\mathcal H (K) \to K</math> that sends <math>\mathcal H (\sigma^n)</math> back to <math>\sigma^n</math> induces a surjection on [[Homology (mathematics)|homology]].

It follows in particular that if <math>K</math> is a closed orientable <math>n</math>-[[manifold]], then so is <math>\mathcal H (K)</math>.

== Examples ==
The following are some examples of common hyperbolization procedures.

=== Strict hyperbolization ===
In <ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Charney |first1=Ruth M. |last2=Davis |first2=Michael W. |date=1995-04-01 |title=Strict hyperbolization |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/004093839400027I |journal=Topology |volume=34 |issue=2 |pages=329–350 |doi=10.1016/0040-9383(94)00027-I |issn=0040-9383|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Charney and Davis introduced a hyperbolization procedure for which <math>\mathcal H (K)</math> is locally CAT(-1). In particular, when <math>K
</math> is compact, the fundamental group <math>\pi_1(\mathcal H (K))</math> is a [[Hyperbolic group|Gromov hyperbolic group]]. The hyperbolizing cell in this procedure is a real [[hyperbolic manifold]] with boundary and corners constructed via arithmetic methods.

=== Riemannian hyperbolization ===
In <ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Ontaneda |first=Pedro |date=2020-06-01 |title=Riemannian hyperbolization |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10240-020-00113-1 |journal=Publications mathématiques de l'IHÉS |language=en |volume=131 |issue=1 |pages=1–72 |doi=10.1007/s10240-020-00113-1 |arxiv=1406.1730 |issn=1618-1913}}</ref> Ontaneda showed that if K is a smooth triangulation of a smooth manifold, then the strict hyperbolization procedure of Charney-Davis<ref name=":0" /> can be refined to ensure that <math>\mathcal H (K)</math> is a smooth manifold and that it admits a Riemannian metric of negative [[sectional curvature]]. Moreover, it is possible to pinch the curvature arbitrarily close to <math>-1</math>.

=== Relative hyperbolization ===
Any hyperbolization procedure <math>\mathcal H</math> admits a relative version, which allows to work relatively to a subcomplex, i.e., keep it unaltered under the hyperbolization.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Davis |first1=Michael W. |last2=Januszkiewicz |first2=Tadeusz |last3=Weinberger |first3=Shmuel |date=2001-07-01 |title=Relative Hyperbolization and Aspherical Bordisms: An Addendum to "Hyperbolization of Polyhedra" |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/journal-of-differential-geometry/volume-58/issue-3/Relative-Hyperbolization-and-Aspherical-Bordisms--An-Addendum-to-Hyperbolization/10.4310/jdg/1090348358.full |journal=Journal of Differential Geometry |volume=58 |issue=3 |doi=10.4310/jdg/1090348358 |issn=0022-040X}}</ref> More precisely, if <math>L\subseteq K</math> is a subcomplex, then one can attach to <math>K</math> the [[Cone (topology)|cone]] over <math>L</math>, apply the hyperbolization procedure to the coned-off complex, and the remove a small neighborhood of the cone point. Thanks to axiom (3) above, the link of the cone point is a copy of <math>L</math>, so removing a small neighborhood of the cone point results in a boundary component homeomorphic to <math>L</math>.

If <math>\mathcal H</math> is the strict hyperbolization of Charney-Davis, then Belegradek showed that the relative version of <math>\mathcal H</math> results in a space whose fundamental group is [[Relatively hyperbolic group|hyperbolic relative]] to <math>\pi_1(K)</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Belegradek |first=Igor |date=2007-10-01 |title=Aspherical manifolds with relatively hyperbolic fundamental groups |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10711-007-9199-8 |journal=Geometriae Dedicata |language=en |volume=129 |issue=1 |pages=119–144 |doi=10.1007/s10711-007-9199-8 |arxiv=math/0509490 |issn=1572-9168}}</ref>

== Applications ==
The following are some classical applications of hyperbolization procedures. The general recipe consists in constructing a complex or manifold with some desired topological features, and then applying a hyperbolization procedure to infuse it with non-positive or negative curvature. Depending on which procedure is used, one can get more geometric control on the output.

# Every triangulable manifold is [[Cobordism|cobordant]] to a triangulable aspherical manifold.<ref name=":1" /> Namely, if <math>M</math> is a triangulable manifold, let <math>\mathcal H(M)</math> denote the hyperbolization of <math>M</math> with respect to some triangulation. Then <math>M</math> and <math>\mathcal H (M)</math> are cobordant. The cobordism is obtained by applying <math>\mathcal H</math> to the cone over <math>M</math>, and then removing a small open neighborhood of the cone point. Using strict hyperbolization, <math>\mathcal H (M)</math> can be chosen to admit a topological metric of negative curvature.<ref name=":0" /> If <math>M</math> is a smooth manifold, then <math>\mathcal H (M)</math>, the metric, and the cobordism can even be taken to be smooth.<ref name=":2" />
# For any <math>n \geq 5</math> there are a closed <math>n</math>-manifold <math>N</math> with a topological metric of negative curvature whose universal cover is not homeomorphic to <math>\mathbb R^n</math>, and also a closed <math>n</math>-manifold <math>N</math> with a topological metric of negative curvature whose universal cover is homeomorphic to <math>\mathbb R^n</math>, but whose [[Gromov boundary|ideal boundary]] is not homeomorphic to the sphere <math>S^{n-1}</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Davis |first1=Michael W. |last2=Januszkiewicz |first2=Tadeusz |date=1991-01-01 |title=Hyperbolization of polyhedra |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/journal-of-differential-geometry/volume-34/issue-2/Hyperbolization-of-polyhedra/10.4310/jdg/1214447212.full |journal=Journal of Differential Geometry |volume=34 |issue=2 |doi=10.4310/jdg/1214447212 |issn=0022-040X}}</ref><ref name=":0" /> 
# For any <math>n \geq 4</math> and for any <math>\varepsilon > 0</math> there exists a closed Riemannian <math>n</math>-manifold <math>N</math> such that all the [[sectional curvature]]s of <math>N</math> are in <math>[-1-\varepsilon, -1]</math>, but <math>N</math> is not homeomorphic to a locally [[symmetric space]].<ref name=":2" /> In particular, <math>\pi_1(N)</math> is a [[Hyperbolic group|Gromov hyperbolic]] group whose [[Gromov boundary]] is a sphere, but <math>\pi_1(N)</math> is not isomorphic to a uniform [[Lattice (discrete subgroup)|lattice]] in a [[Lie group]] of rank 1.
# If <math>M</math> is a closed orientable [[Piecewise linear manifold|PL-manifold]] that is the boundary of another PL-manifold, then there is a [[Hyperbolic group|Gromov hyperbolic]] group <math>G</math> whose [[Gromov boundary]] is the tree of manifolds defined by <math>M</math>, i.e., a certain [[inverse limit]] of connected sums of <math>M</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Świątkowski |first=Jacek |date=2020-09-23 |title=Trees of manifolds as boundaries of spaces and groups |url=https://msp.org/gt/2020/24-2/p02.xhtml |journal=Geometry & Topology |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=593–622 |doi=10.2140/gt.2020.24.593 |arxiv=1304.5067 |issn=1364-0380}}</ref>
